How to empower through representation

Remember Schoolhouse Rock? How a bill becomes a law?

Well, that was lying to you for educational purposes. The reality is much more complicated. It's political — but there's also room for you. At least, through Square Party there is. We give you the resources you need to understand how laws and regulations affect your life, and how you can help improve them.

This project applies a People's Assembly framework to Pennsylvania's 3rd Congressional District — Philadelphia plus parts of Delaware and Montgomery Counties. The framework is twenty-six policy domains, organized to cover everything government touches. For each one, we document what the law says, how it actually runs in PA-3, and where the two diverge.

The methodology is the same across all twenty-six: five lenses (statutory architecture, administrative implementation, constituent experience, gap analysis, and statutory-vs-administrative durability), applied uniformly so readers can compare across domains. Read the methodology in full →

Policy proposals are out of scope on these analytical pages. They get generated downstream by contributors through the propose tier. Surfacing the gap is the job of the analysis; closing it is the job of whoever does the proposing.

The framework — domains as topical seats of a People's Assembly — is the Square Party-level idea this project applies in one place. Express interest in any of the topical seats →

The twenty-six domains, in PA-3

State indicators describe analytical state, not domain importance. Published domains have verified PA-3 content. In review is drafted but unchecked. Drafting is research underway. Planned is scaffolded, not yet researched. The honest current state: one domain is being adapted from a separate research document; the rest are scaffolded and await contributors.

  • Identity→

    Citizenship, immigration, vital records, legal personhood, identification systems, the architecture of \"who counts as what\" for governmental purposes.

  • Civil Rights→

    The cross-cutting anti-discrimination enforcement architecture — Titles VI, VII, IX, ADA, FHA, Section 504, Voting Rights Act, and the federal enforcement bodies that operate under them.

  • Elections→

    The architecture of representation itself — Voting Rights Act, NVRA, HAVA, state election administration, voter registration, redistricting, campaign finance, ballot access, election security.

  • Public Health→

    Disease surveillance, public health agencies, vaccination, health emergencies, environmental health, the population-level health apparatus distinct from individual medical care.

  • Mental Health→

    Mental health care access, mental health parity, crisis response systems, public mental health services, the institutional architecture for serious mental illness.

  • Healthcare→

    Provider-side institutional architecture and the regulatory regimes governing it — hospitals, FQHCs, Medicare delivery-payment, ACA marketplaces, provider licensure.

  • Food & Drugs→

    Food safety, drug regulation, supply chains for both, the FDA's regulatory domain, medical device regulation, the gray areas (supplements, off-label).

  • Veterans→

    Title 38 architecture — VA healthcare system, GI Bill / Post-9/11 education benefits, USERRA, veteran preference in employment, VBA disability and pension benefits.

  • Public Benefits→

    Income support, SNAP, TANF, housing assistance, social insurance — the architecture of public support for people whose circumstances put them outside what the labor market alone provides.

  • Labor→

    Wages, working conditions, unions and collective bargaining, workplace safety, unemployment insurance, gig and platform work, the full architecture of the employer-employee relationship.

  • Finance & TaxDrafting→

    Tax policy, public finance, banking regulation, the fiscal architecture across federal, state, and local layers.

  • Land & Property→

    Real property law, zoning, eminent domain, housing, public land, the legal infrastructure of who owns what and what they can do with it.

  • Infrastructure→

    Roads, transit, water systems, ports, bridges, the built environment that everyone uses regardless of whether they think about it.

  • Energy→

    Electricity grid, fuels, energy policy, transition planning, utility regulation, the public-private architecture of energy delivery.

  • Environment→

    Air, water, lands, wildlife, climate policy, environmental regulation across federal, state, and local layers.

  • Agriculture→

    Farms, food systems at the source, agricultural labor, USDA programs, water for irrigation, soil and land use.

  • Education→

    Schools from pre-K through higher education, curriculum, funding formulas, accreditation, the public/private/charter mix, special education, libraries qua educational institutions.

  • Arts & Sciences→

    Public funding and infrastructure for the arts, the sciences, and the public communication of both — grants, institutions, public broadcasting, research universities qua research.

  • Internet & Telecom→

    Broadband access, telecommunications, internet governance, public digital services, the public-private edges of digital infrastructure.

  • Public Records→

    Public records, archives, FOIA, the census, historical preservation, transparency law, the records infrastructure that makes everything else possible to verify.

  • Commerce→

    Trade regulation, antitrust, business formation, industrial policy, supply chains, sector-specific regulation outside the carve-outs that have their own domains.

  • Gambling & Fraud→

    Casino and gambling regulation, financial crime, securities fraud, public corruption — the regulatory and enforcement architecture for the kinds of harm that don't show up in violent crime statistics.

  • Public Safety→

    Policing, prosecution, corrections, courts, national security, intelligence, the full enforcement and adjudication apparatus.

  • Emergency Mgmt.→

    Disaster preparedness and response, FEMA, civil defense, mutual aid, the layered federal/state/local emergency apparatus.

  • Government Itself→

    How government runs itself — civil service, procurement, transparency, internal accountability, the meta-domain that shapes how every other domain actually functions.

  • Foreign Policy→

    Diplomacy, foreign aid, international agreements, military action abroad, the institutional architecture of how the U.S. interacts with the rest of the world.

Help us make our laws better!

Rather than rely on paid lobbyists and well-connected staffers and who knows who else, let's just start doing it.

It's a big job. But we can break it down into small parts and let anyone learn as much or as little as they want and still participate meaningfully.

The approach I'm trying is to map the power structures onto the people they actually affect — that's you.

In theory, we can develop proposals for new regulations or laws (as well as getting rid of ones that have no reasonable purpose). But first, the framework needs human verification. Statistics are easy to check; this won't work unless people go talk to other people in the world and report back. Surveys and other tools are coming, but for now you can see how the mapping of power to representation by constituents is coming along.

GitHub is open for updates and corrections to existing information. Discussions about future areas can be started with an issue. More user-friendly options for interaction will be added after the development phase.

How to engage

Verify & contribute

This project gets better when readers push back on it. Every page is editable, every change is tracked, every contributor is credited at whatever level of identity they choose.

  1. Read

    No account needed. Read anything on the site, follow citations, decide for yourself whether the analysis holds.

  2. Contribute

    Spot a factual error, missing source, or framing problem? Open a pull request on GitHub. Quick fixes, source additions, narrative edits — all welcome.

    How to contribute →

  3. Propose

    Bigger ideas — a new sub-domain analysis, a constituent profile, a policy proposal — go through a longer review. Same PR mechanism, more conversation around it.

    How to propose →

Privacy: every contribution is attributed at the level you pick — anonymous, first name + neighborhood, full name + neighborhood, or full name with link. Privacy options →
